<reason>Both sides were strong, but B built the cleaner path to victory. A's central move — that B's remediation-plus-backstop model "restates the motion" — was genuinely dangerous, but B neutralized it with the debate's most important distinction: the motion fines outcomes (repeated failure), while B's model fines conduct (refusal after binding, monitored milestones). B named a concrete class the motion punishes and its model spares — the good-faith hospital mid-remediation whose site still fails — and repeated it across four speeches. A's answers (progress defense, earmarked fines, binary-only triggers) were each characterized with some force as redesigns that convert the trigger from failure to refusal, and B also turned A's own OSHA/tax analogies. A's closing claimed B "never named" the extra punished actor, which misdescribes the record and undercut A's best argument at the moment it mattered most. A also let the small-provider withdrawal and public-body circularity threads lapse after Rebuttal 1, while B's trigger dilemma (binary = theater cover, judgment-laden = arbitrariness) was only partially answered by a narrowing move B exploited. Both sides were disciplined, well-grounded, and format-compliant; B simply kept the decisive clash sharper and described the exchange more accurately.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 (B2.1): the failure-vs-refusal distinction — strict liability on outcome versus penalties for defiance of an order — dissolved A's "you've conceded the motion" move and set the frame A never escaped, later reinforced when B4.6 turned A's OSHA/tax analogies into further proof that A's defensible version of the motion was B's mechanism in different vocabulary.</best_rebuttal>
